**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I tried to write a thousand words, I stared at the blank page like it was a vast, uncharted ocean. Where do I begin? Do I dive into the depths of memory, or do I let my fingers wander across the keys like aimless travelers? A thousand words is both nothing and everything—enough to build a world, but never enough to say all that needs saying.

I think about the things I’ve left unsaid. The way my grandmother’s hands smelled like flour and lavender when she pulled me into her kitchen, pressing warm cookies into my palms. The way the city hums at 3 a.m., when the drunkards have gone home and the bakers are just waking up. The way grief sits in your chest like a stone you can’t cough up, no matter how hard you try.

Words are strange creatures. They can be precise as a surgeon’s scalpel or blunt as a hammer. They can mend or they can wound. And sometimes, they do both at once. I’ve written love letters that felt like prayers, sentences so raw I had to look away from the screen. I’ve written angry rants that burned holes in the paper, only to tear them up the next morning, ashamed.

There’s a myth that writing is solitary, but I don’t believe that. Every word I put down is a conversation—with myself, with the reader I imagine, with the ghosts of every writer who ever made me feel less alone. These thousand words are a hand reaching out, hoping someone, somewhere, will reach back.

Maybe that’s why we write—to prove we were here. That we felt, we stumbled, we loved, we raged. That we saw the way the light slanting through the blinds turns the dust in the air into something holy. That we noticed.

And yet, for all the weight we give words, they’re just symbols. Ink on a page. Pixels on a screen. They mean nothing until someone reads them, until a mind and a heart alchemize them into meaning. That’s the magic and the terror of it: you can pour your soul into a thousand words, and they might still be met with silence. Or worse—misunderstanding.

But here’s the thing: you write anyway.

You write because the alternative is to let the thoughts rot inside you, to let the stories wither unspoken. You write because sometimes the only way to make sense of the chaos is to shape it into sentences. You write because, in the act of creation, you become a little less afraid of the world.

So here I am, 500 words in, and I realize I don’t know where this is going. That’s the beauty of it. Writing isn’t about control; it’s about surrender. Letting the words take you where they will. Maybe the next 500 will be a rant about the absurdity of modern life, or a list of small joys I’m afraid to forget, or a confession I’ve never voiced aloud.

Or maybe they’ll just be more words about words. A meta spiral, a writer writing about writing, because what else is there, really? We are the sum of our stories, the things we tell and the things we keep buried. And if I can string together a thousand words—messy, imperfect, honest—then maybe, just maybe, I’ve done something true.

The cursor blinks. The page is no longer blank. And that’s enough. For now.
